content: The following is a guide for creating a WikiDoc Journal Landmark Trial page. A trial page is a comprehensive collection of all relevant information about a clinical study, including a detailed breakdown of its design and findings. Each study is composed of various CONSORT checklist items, such as trial design, interventions, outcomes, randomization, statistical methods, and limitations. These pages are designed to help users efficiently access the information they need, facilitate navigation of the study of interest, and ensure completeness and consistency across WikiDoc pages. Below are the key sections and their descriptions: 1. Complete Title of Study: This section should include the full name of the study in the first sentence. It should not include the study acronym. 2. Study Acronym: This section should include the study acronym, which may not necessarily be the initials of the study title. For example, the acronym RALES stands for Randomized Aldactone Evaluation Study for congestive heart failure, while the full title of the study is The effect of spironolactone on morbidity and mortality in patients with severe heart failure. 3. Principal Investigator, Co-investigators, and Collaborating Institutions: This section should list the principal investigator, co-investigators, and collaborating institutions involved in the study. It should not include funding sources. 4. Overview: This section provides a general overview of the trial and should include the study acronym in the first sentence. It serves as a summary of all the overview statements below it. 5. Disease State(s) Studied: This section should list all the major diseases studied in the trial, including the primary outcome diseases. 6. Study Design: This section should describe the study setting (e.g., multicenter or single-center, with the number of sites and countries if available), type of blinding (e.g., single-blind, double-blind, open-label), design (e.g., parallel arms, crossover, factorial, delayed-start), and sample size (total number of randomized patients). This information can typically be found in the CONSORT flowchart, abstract, or study methods section. 7. Study Duration and Time-points: This section should include the total study duration, participant enrollment period, study start date, follow-up duration, and study visits (time-points where primary outcomes are assessed). It should also include stoppage criteria and reasons, if available. 8. Interventions: This section should describe all treatment arms studied in the trial, including both active comparator and experimental arms. It should specify the number of arms, experimental treatments, and active comparator/standard treatments. 9. Study Measures: This section should detail the study measures used in the trial. Measures refer to the items in a research study to which participants respond. For example, if the outcome measurement is cholesterol levels, it should specify the unit of measurement (e.g., milligrams per deciliter of blood) and the frequency of assessment. 10. Primary Endpoint: This section describes the primary endpoint of the clinical trial, which is the main reason for randomizing subjects and powering the trial. It may include composite endpoints but should not include any statistical reports. 11. Secondary Endpoints: This section describes the secondary endpoints of the trial, which are analyzed post hoc and may not be powered or randomized. It should list all secondary outcomes but exclude statistical reports. 12. Inclusion Criteria: This section outlines the characteristics that prospective subjects must have to be included in the study. 13. Exclusion Criteria: This section outlines the characteristics that disqualify subjects from being included in the study. 14. Outcome: Primary Endpoint: This section should describe the primary endpoint outcome results, comparing experimental and control arms. It should include the statistical report (e.g., relative risk, hazard ratio, odds ratio, standardized mean difference, p-value, number needed to treat). 15. Outcome: Secondary Endpoint: This section should describe the secondary endpoint outcome results, comparing experimental and control arms. It should include the statistical report. 16. Outcome: Exploratory Endpoints: This section should describe the exploratory endpoint outcome results, comparing experimental and control arms. It should include the statistical report. 17. Subgroup Analysis: This section should describe the subgroup analysis, comparing experimental and control arms. It should include the statistical report. 18. Outcome: Safety Endpoints: This section should describe the safety endpoint outcome results, comparing experimental and control arms. It should include the statistical report (e.g., relative risk, hazard ratio, odds ratio, standardized mean difference, p-value, number needed to harm). 19. Statistical Methods: This section describes the statistical methods used in the clinical trial. It should include sample size calculation (if available), statistical tests used (e.g., t-test, MANOVA, ANOVA, linear regression, chi-squared, correlation), descriptive statistics, power, and effect size. It should also specify the level of significance and the type of analysis (e.g., intention-to-treat or per-protocol). 20. Conclusions: This section summarizes the conclusions of the clinical trial. It should state whether the active intervention is superior, inferior, or equivalent to the control intervention in achieving the primary outcome. It should also indicate whether the results were positive or negative for the primary endpoint. 21. Discussion and Limitations of the Trial: This section discusses the trial's findings, limitations, potential sources of bias, imprecision, and, if relevant, the multiplicity of analyses. 22. Commentary: This section provides personal comments about the study. 23. Slides: This section includes a link to download slides from the WikiDoc journal club on the trial.
